Print Email Copy Link Add KFF on Google Key Points In September 2025, the State Department released the America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), its new approach for U.S. engagement in global health, anchored to bilateral agreements negotiated directly with countries (through memoranda of understanding, or MOUs), although limited information is available on their status. To supplement and support MOU implementation, the State Department is also using an Annual Program Statement (APS) mechanism, an open-ended competitive funding opportunity, to solicit applications in support of AFGHS goals. To shed greater light on U.S. global health efforts under the AFGHS, this analysis examines the Advancing Global Health APS (AGH/APS) award opportunities announced to date by looking at how funding may be directed across countries and selected areas of global health programming, painting a fuller picture of how continued U.S. global health investment may look in a post-USAID foreign aid landscape. The State Department anticipates using the AGH/APS to provide up to $4.5 billion across four funding windows from March 2026 to February 2027. A range of entities are eligible to apply for funding, including governments and non-governmental organizations, and funding opportunities are made available through specific addenda. To date, 12 addenda have been released across three funding rounds, totaling up to $1.43 billion and representing up to 122 possible awards. Seven of the 12 are focused on specific MOU countries – Cameroon, Cote d’Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, the Philippines, and Uganda. Five are focused on specific health areas – child development, care, and protection; neglected tropical diseases (NTDs); nutrition; population-based surveys and surveillance; and rapid outbreak response (the NTDs and nutrition addenda identify specific geographic areas and countries for support). Objectives and activities across the addenda are varied and range from enhancing the delivery of health services across disease programs; supporting high-impact NTD interventions; strengthening the systems and workforce that protect vulnerable children through improved laws, policies, and services; and strengthening global health security through improved infection prevention and control, immunization for outbreak response, point-of-entry screening, and risk communication. Some addenda include mentions of key, focus, and vulnerable populations (including women and children, and people living with HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria). These findings provide insight into how the U.S. intends to further operationalize its global health efforts under the AFGHS, including which MOU countries will be the focus of this work, which global health areas have been selected for cross-cutting support, and what objectives and activities might be supported with more focused, additional support within and beyond MOU countries. Still, the APS process remains underway, and additional addenda are expected as part of the last funding round. At this time, no awards have been publicly announced, and it is not known what will actually be funded. How this APS mechanism and specific awards ultimately operate to support or supplement the MOUs and other aspects of the AFGHS will be important to monitor going forward. Introduction Starting early on during his second administration, President Trump made a number of sweeping changes to U.S. foreign aid , which reverberated across U.S. and broader global health efforts. These included the reduction in the number of supported projects and organizations, dissolution of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and the shifting of responsibility for remaining efforts to the State Department. In September 2025, following months of uncertainty, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy (AFGHS), outlining a fundamental shift in how the U.S. is planning to carry out its global health work. This new approach is anchored to bilateral agreements negotiated directly with countries receiving U.S. global health assistance. To date, 36 such agreements, through Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) totaling $26.7 billion, have been signed (although limited information is available on their status), with their implementation plans to come. These bilateral agreements each identify and prioritize global health needs to be financed jointly by the U.S. and partner country, with the U.S. committing $15.9 billion and partner countries committing to co-invest $10.3 billion so far. 1 The State Department has indicated that a main mechanism for implementing the MOUs will be through government-to-government (G2G) funding agreements, although these are still nascent and expected to take some time to develop. As such, the Department has also released – through an “Annual Program Statement” (APS), an open-ended competitive funding mechanism – a supplemental framework to support MOU implementation called the “ Advancing Global Health APS ” (AGH/APS) to solicit applications in support of AFGHS goals.
Announced in March 2026, the State Department anticipates using the AGH/APS to provide up to $4.5 billion (subject to the availability of funds) over four funding windows from March 2026 through February 2027, with awards ranging from $500,000 to $250 million over 5 years. Some of the funding will be part of a country’s overall MOU funding envelope, while other funding may sit outside this envelope. Eligible applicants are U.S. and foreign private for-profit enterprises; U.S. and foreign public and private institutions of higher education; U.S and foreign organizations, including faith-based organizations; Public International Organizations (PIOs); and governmental institutions.
To shed greater light on U.S. global health efforts under the AFGHS, this policy brief provides an analysis of the AGH/APS award opportunities (“addenda”) announced to date by looking at how funding may be directed across countries and selected areas of global health programming, painting a fuller picture of how continued U.S. global health investment may look in a post-USAID foreign aid landscape.
As of November 2026, 12 addenda with up to 122 possible awards have been announced across three funding rounds, totaling up to $1.43 billion (see Box 1 ). This funding represents almost a third (32%) of the anticipated funding of $4.5 billion. Addenda include both country- and area-specific solicitations.
